content.title: About
content.content: Wasabi paste is a spicy condiment made from the root of the wasabi plant (Wasabia japonica) or from a blend of horseradish, mustard, and food coloring. The paste is bright green, aromatic, and delivers a sharp, slightly sweet heat that hits the nose as well as the palate.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: True wasabi is cultivated in Japan, mainly in the cool, humid mountain streams of Honshu.
Only about 5 % of commercially available wasabi products are 100 % genuine; most are horseradish‑based imitations.
Traditionally it is served with sushi and sashimi to enhance the flavor of raw fish and cleanse the palate.
The root contains isothiocyanates, which give wasabi its characteristic heat and aroma.
Wasabi has natural antibacterial properties, making it a useful accompaniment in sushi bars.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Isothiocyanates in wasabi help neutralize free radicals, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Compounds in the paste stimulate immune‑cell activity and may boost the body’s defense mechanisms.

items.title: Antibacterial action
items.content: Wasabi inhibits the growth of certain pathogenic bacteria, which is beneficial when eating raw fish.

items.title: Digestive stimulation
items.content: The sharp flavor promotes gastric juice secretion, aiding digestion.

items.title: Cardiovascular health
items.content: Studies suggest isothiocyanates can improve lipid profiles and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to wasabi or its substitutes.

items.title: Mucosal irritation
items.content: Large amounts of the hot paste can cause burning sensations in the mouth, stomach, or intestines.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ready‑made commercial pastes often contain salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Fake product
items.content: Horseradish‑based imitations may include artificial colors and preservatives that lack the health benefits of true wasabi.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Wasabi paste is typically served in small dollops alongside sushi, sashimi, rolls, or grilled dishes. It can be stirred into sauces, marinades, soups, and salads for extra heat. When using a horseradish imitation, a splash of lemon juice adds a brighter flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the paste in a sealed jar in the refrigerator. Properly stored, it retains its flavor for up to 6 months. Discard if the aroma becomes overly sharp or the color fades.
